n: Samuel reminds Saul that the Lord made him king through Samuel, so he must now listen carefully to the Lord's words. This chapter is a test of Saul's obedience.

f.w: hearken thou unto the voice of the words of the LORD

n: The Lord recalls how Amalek attacked Israel's weak and weary stragglers after the Exodus. Judgment on Amalek had been promised long before.

f.w: that which Amalek did to Israel

n: Saul is commanded to devote Amalek to complete destruction — people and animals. This is one of scripture's most troubling commands; it reflects ancient “holy war,” and readers have long wrestled with it humbly. The point in the story is Saul's obedience.

f.g: Hebrew ḥerem — to devote something entirely to God by destruction, keeping nothing as plunder.

n: Saul gathers a large army at Telaim in the south, again counting Judah separately.

f.g: A place in southern Judah, perhaps the same as Telem.

n: Saul approaches an Amalekite city and sets an ambush in the valley.
Saul warns the Kenites living among the Amalekites to leave, because they had been kind to Israel during the Exodus. Moses' father-in-law was a Kenite.
Saul defeats the Amalekites across a wide region, from Havilah to Shur near Egypt's border.

f.g: A desert region east of Egypt.

n: Saul captures Agag the Amalekite king alive while destroying the people. Sparing the king may have been for show, as a trophy of victory.

f.g: Possibly a royal title among the Amalekites.

n: Saul and his men spare Agag and the best animals and goods, destroying only what was worthless. Partial obedience: they kept what they wanted and destroyed what they didn't.

f.g: fattened animals
worthless and rejected

n: The Lord speaks to Samuel about Saul's disobedience.

The Lord says He regrets making Saul king because Saul has turned away. Samuel is deeply grieved and prays all night. The Joseph Smith Translation adjusts this verse so that Saul is the one who has not repented.

f.g: “Repent” here means to regret or be grieved; the JST wording places the failure to repent on Saul.

f.w: he cried unto the LORD all night

n: Samuel learns that Saul went to Carmel and set up a monument to himself before going down to Gilgal. Saul is honoring himself, not God.

f.g: A town in southern Judah, not Mount Carmel in the north.
Literally “a hand” — a monument or memorial pillar.

n: Saul greets Samuel cheerfully, claiming he has obeyed the Lord's command — either self-deceived or trying to deceive Samuel.
Samuel's reply is sharp and almost ironic: then what is all this bleating and mooing I hear? The evidence of disobedience is loud and clear.

f.g: mooing

n: Saul blames “the people” and offers a religious excuse: they spared the best animals to sacrifice to the Lord. Note he says “thy God,” not “my God.”

f.g: Saul shifts responsibility away from himself.

n: Samuel cuts Saul off: “Stop! Let me tell you what the Lord told me last night.” Saul says, “Speak.”

f.g: Stop, be quiet

n: Samuel reminds Saul that he was once humble and small in his own eyes, yet the Lord made him king. Pride has crept in since then.
The Lord's command was clear: go and completely destroy the Amalekites.
So why did Saul not obey, but rushed on the plunder and did evil in the Lord's sight?

f.g: swoop down greedily on the plunder

n: Saul insists again that he obeyed, listing what he did right while ignoring what he didn't. Self-justification keeps him from true repentance.

f.w: I have obeyed the voice of the LORD

n: Again he blames the people for taking the best of the spoil and adds that it was for sacrifice at Gilgal.
Samuel declares a timeless principle: the Lord wants obedience more than sacrifices. Rituals mean little when the heart is disobedient.

f.w: to obey is better than sacrifice

f.g: the choicest part of an offering

n: Rebellion and stubbornness are as serious as witchcraft and idolatry, because they put self above God. Since Saul rejected God's word, God rejects him as king.

f.g: divination — seeking guidance from forbidden sources
arrogance, insistence on one's own way

n: Saul finally admits his sin and the real reason: he feared the people and listened to them instead of God. Fear of others' opinions often drives disobedience.
Saul asks for pardon and for Samuel to return with him to worship. His concern seems more for appearances than for his relationship with God (see verse 30).
Samuel refuses: Saul has rejected the Lord's word, and the Lord has rejected him as king.
As Samuel turns to go, Saul grabs the hem of Samuel's robe and it tears.

f.g: the hem or corner of his robe

n: Samuel turns the torn robe into a living prophecy: the Lord has torn the kingdom from Saul today and given it to someone better — David.

f.g: another person, a fellow Israelite

n: God, the “Strength of Israel,” does not lie or change His mind like a human. His decision about Saul is final.

f.g: A title for God; it can also mean “the Glory” or “Eternal One of Israel.”

f.w: he is not a man, that he should repent

n: Saul confesses again but asks Samuel to honor him in front of the elders. He still cares most about saving face.
Samuel goes back with Saul, and Saul worships the Lord. Samuel may have returned to deal with Agag himself.
Samuel summons Agag, who comes confidently, thinking the danger of death has passed.

f.g: Possibly “cheerfully” or “in chains”; the Hebrew is uncertain.

n: Samuel declares that as Agag's sword made many mothers childless, so his own mother will be childless. Samuel carries out the judgment Saul neglected.

f.g: executed him
as a judicial act in God's presence

n: Samuel and Saul part ways — Samuel to Ramah, Saul to his home in Gibeah.
Samuel never visits Saul again in life, but he grieves for him. The Lord regretted making Saul king — the JST again revises this wording so that God is not said to repent.

f.g: “Repented” means “was grieved” or “regretted”; God's sorrow over a failed servant.
